title.en: Derive the gain of the inverting amplifier
Derive the gain of the non-inverting amplifier

say.en: With an op-amp, the gain no longer depends on the transistors inside. Two resistors decide it, and you can read it straight off their values. In this lesson: Derive the gain of the inverting amplifier.
Derive the gain of the non-inverting amplifier.
Explain the voltage follower.

body.en: The input $V_i$ is applied through $R_1$ to the *inverting* terminal; $R_f$ connects the output back to it; the non-inverting terminal is grounded. The inverting terminal is a virtual ground, so the current through $R_1$ is $I = V_i/R_1$. No current enters the op-amp, so the same current flows through $R_f$: $I = (0 - V_o)/R_f$. Equating, $A_v = V_o/V_i = -R_f/R_1$. The output is 180° out of phase and the input resistance is $R_1$.

narration.en: For the inverting amplifier the gain is minus Rf over R1. The output is inverted, and the input resistance is R1.
narration.kn: ಇನ್ವರ್ಟಿಂಗ್ ವರ್ಧಕದ ವರ್ಧನೆ Av = −Rf/R1. ಔಟ್‌ಪುಟ್ 180° ತಿರುಗಿರುತ್ತದೆ; ಇನ್‌ಪುಟ್ ರೋಧ R1.

say.en: Input goes through R1 to the inverting terminal; Rf returns the output to the same point. The non-inverting terminal is grounded.
Point X is a virtual ground, so the current through R1 is Vi over R1, and it all flows on through Rf. That gives the gain minus Rf over R1.
Feed the input to the plus terminal instead and the gain is one plus Rf over R1, in phase. With Rf zero it becomes a voltage follower.

body.en: In the *non-inverting amplifier* the input goes to the + terminal, and $R_f$ with $R_1$ (to ground) feed back a fraction $R_1/(R_1+R_f)$ of the output to the − terminal. Since $V_- \approx V_+ = V_i$, $V_o = V_i(1 + R_f/R_1)$, so $A_v = 1 + R_f/R_1$, in phase, with a very high input resistance. With $R_f = 0$ and $R_1$ removed, $A_v = 1$: the voltage follower, a buffer with very high input and very low output resistance. In practice the output is limited to about ±13 V with a ±15 V supply (saturation).

narration.en: For the non-inverting amplifier the gain is one plus Rf over R1, in phase. The voltage follower has a gain of exactly one and is used as a buffer.

heading.en: Op-amp Basics: IC 741, Ideal Op-amp, Inverting and Non-inverting Amplifiers

tagline.en: What an op-amp is, its internal blocks and IC 741 pins, ideal versus practical characteristics, CMRR and slew rate, the virtual ground, and the derivation of inverting and non-inverting gain.

myth.en: With A_OL = 2 × 10⁵, an input of 1 mV gives an output of 200 V.

truth.en: The output can never go beyond the saturation voltage (about ±13 V on ±15 V supplies). Open-loop, 1 mV already drives a 741 into saturation, which is why linear circuits always use negative feedback. The formula V_o = A_OL V_d holds only while the output is inside the supply limits. Energy for the output comes from the supply, so the output cannot exceed it.

say.en: Op-amp: direct-coupled, high-gain differential amplifier; V_o = A_OL(V₊ − V₋), limited by ±V_sat.
IC 741 pins: 2 inverting, 3 non-inverting, 6 output, 7 +V_CC, 4 −V_EE, 1 and 5 offset null.
Ideal: infinite gain, input resistance, bandwidth, CMRR and slew rate; zero output resistance.
Inverting: A_v = −R_f/R₁. Non-inverting: A_v = 1 + R_f/R₁.
CMRR = A_d/A_cm; slew rate limits f_max = SR/(2πV_m).

say.en: Let us work this out together. R1 equals 10 k ohms, Rf equals 100 k ohms and Vi equals 0.5 volts. Find the output as a an inverting amplifier, b a non-inverting amplifier.
a Av equals minus 100 over 10 equals minus 10, so Vo equals minus 10 times 0.5 equals minus 5 volts.
b Av equals 1 plus 100 over 10 equals 11, so Vo equals 11 times 0.5 equals 5.5 volts.
So the answer is a minus 5 volts, b plus 5.5 volts.

problem.en: An inverting amplifier with gain −10 runs from ±15 V (saturation ±13 V). Find the output for Vi = 2 V.

steps.en: The output cannot go below −13 V, so it saturates.
Vo = −13 V: the input is too large for this gain.

say.en: Let us work this out together. An inverting amplifier with gain minus 10 runs from plus or minus 15 volts (saturation plus or minus 13 volts). Find the output for Vi equals 2 volts.
Ideal Vo equals minus 10 times 2 equals minus 20 volts.
The output cannot go below minus 13 volts, so it saturates.
Vo equals minus 13 volts: the input is too large for this gain.
So the answer is minus 13 volts saturated.

homework.en: Derive the voltage gain of an op-amp non-inverting amplifier with a neat circuit diagram.

narration.en: Recap. Inverting: Av = −Rf/R1, input resistance R1. Non-inverting: Av = 1 + Rf/R1, in phase. Voltage follower: Av = 1, used as a buffer. Output cannot exceed the saturation voltage.
narration.kn: ಪುನರಾವರ್ತನೆ. ಇನ್ವರ್ಟಿಂಗ್: Av = −Rf/R1, ಇನ್‌ಪುಟ್ ರೋಧ R1. ನಾನ್-ಇನ್ವರ್ಟಿಂಗ್: Av = 1 + Rf/R1, ಒಂದೇ ಹಂತ. ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಫಾಲೋವರ್: Av = 1, ಬಫರ್. ಔಟ್‌ಪುಟ್ ಸ್ಯಾಚುರೇಶನ್ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಮೀರಲಾರದು.

say.en: Let us recall the key ideas. Inverting: Av equals -Rf over R1, input resistance R1.
say.kn: ಮುಖ್ಯ ಅಂಶಗಳನ್ನು ನೆನಪಿಸಿಕೊಳ್ಳೋಣ. ಇನ್ವರ್ಟಿಂಗ್: Av equals -Rf over R1, ಇನ್‌ಪುಟ್ ರೋಧ R1.

say.en: Non-inverting: Av equals 1 plus Rf over R1, in phase.
say.kn: ನಾನ್-ಇನ್ವರ್ಟಿಂಗ್: Av equals 1 plus Rf over R1, ಒಂದೇ ಹಂತ.

say.en: Voltage follower: Av equals 1, used as a buffer.
Output cannot exceed the saturation voltage.
